title: Designing with Magnets
seo_title: Grade 3 Magnet Design Worksheets: Solving Problems with Magnets
standard_text: Define a simple design problem that can be solved by applying scientific ideas about magnets.
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 science worksheets on designing with magnets (NGSS 3-PS2-4): magnetic latches, can sorters and other magnet solutions, criteria and constraints, and testing designs with data. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_sub: Use what you know about magnets: they pull iron and steel, work without touching, and pull harder when closer.
body_html:
How to think about it

Engineers use what they know about magnets to solve problems:

  • Magnets attract iron and steel, so they can latch doors, hold notes and sort steel from aluminum.
  • Magnets work without touching, so they can move toys or lift pins.
  • Closer and stronger magnets pull harder.

A design has criteria (what it must do) and constraints (limits such as cost, time and materials). Test the design, look at the results and improve it.

Example

You need to pick up spilled steel tacks. What tool could you build?

Steel is attracted to magnets.

Answer: a magnet wand

Example

A latch must hold 10 washers and cost less than $3. Design A holds 12 and costs $2. Does it work?

12 ≥ 10

$2 < $3

Answer: Yes, it meets both rules.

Common mistakes

  • Using a magnet to pick up aluminum, plastic or paper.
  • Choosing the strongest design without checking the constraints, like cost.
  • Not testing a design more than once.

faq.a: Magnets can keep doors closed, hold notes on a fridge, sort steel cans from aluminum cans, pick up steel pins and move toys without touching.
Criteria are what a design must do. Constraints are limits such as cost, time and materials.

faq.q: Why must you test a design?
faq.a: Testing shows if the design works. You can use the results to improve it.

items.q: Sam wants to pick up spilled steel pins from a carpet. Which design would work best?
c: a sponge
a wooden ruler
a plastic comb
a magnet wand moved over the carpet
items.e: The pins are steel, so the magnet pulls them up.

items.q: Why would a magnet NOT help sort plastic bottles from glass bottles?
c: Magnets attract only glass.
Bottles are too heavy.
Magnets do not attract plastic or glass.
Magnets attract only plastic.
items.e: Neither material is magnetic.

items.q: Lily wants to hang drawings on a metal fridge door. Which design would work best?
c: small magnets that hold the paper against the door
aluminum foil
glue on the fridge
rubber bands
items.e: The magnets are attracted to the steel door through the paper.

items.q: Sofia's design uses a strong magnet that lifts the steel cans out of the pile to separate steel cans from aluminum cans for recycling. Why does it work?
c: The magnet makes the objects lighter.
Steel is attracted to magnets; aluminum is not.
Magnets attract all materials.
Magnets only work when they are wet.
items.e: Steel is attracted to magnets; aluminum is not.

items.q: Which problem could a magnet help solve?
c: picking up spilled milk
drying wet paper
picking up steel nails that fell in the grass
lifting a plastic cup
items.e: Magnets attract steel.

items.q: Maya's design uses a magnet on the door and a steel plate on the frame to keep a cabinet door from swinging open. Why does it work?

Magnets only work when they are wet.
The magnet pulls on the steel plate and holds the door shut.
The magnet makes the objects lighter.
items.e: The magnet pulls on the steel plate and holds the door shut.

items.q: Which part of a design problem tells what the solution must do?

the materials only

items.e: Criteria are goals; constraints are limits.
